title: Why this lecture?
text:
Why this lecture?
• This chapter now has two connected parts:
• Generative text foundations: tokenizer →ids, causal LM training
(shifted labels), decoding, KV-cache.
• Modern deployment skills: LoRA/QLoRA adaptation and API
integration.
• Pretrained LMs are still too large to fully fine-tune for most student
projects and many industry teams, so parameter-efficient methods
matter.
• Course samples live under DLA/slides/10-modern-llms/samples/
(same chapter as this PDF).

title: Tokenization and vocabulary
text:
Tokenization and vocabulary
Before tensors
• Raw text →tokenizer →integer ids xt ∈{0, . . . , |V| −1} (fixed
vocabulary V).
• Modern LMs often use subword tokenizers (BPE, SentencePiece): fewer
unknown words, variable sequence length per sentence.
• Special tokens (names vary): padding (<pad>), begin/end of sequence
(<bos>, <eos>), unknown (<unk>) — must match between training and
inference checkpoints.
• Practical rule: same tokenizer + same vocab as pretraining when
fine-tuning or loading weights; mixing tokenizers breaks the model.

title: RNN language model
text:
RNN language model
Connection to Chapter 5
• Use an RNN (or LSTM / GRU) to encode prefix w1:t−1 into hidden state
ht.
• At each step:
ht = f (ht−1, Embed(wt−1)),
p(wt | w<t) = Softmax(W ht + b).
• Loss: cross-entropy between predicted distribution and true next token.
• This is a generative model: we can sample full sentences token-by-token.

title: GPT-style causal LM
text:
GPT-style causal LM
Decoder-only stack
• A single stack of L decoder blocks with a causal mask: position t only
attends to tokens ≤t.
• Embedding + positional scheme (learned sinusoids, RoPE,. . . depending
on checkpoint) maps token ids →hidden states H ∈Rn×d.
• After the stack, a language-model head maps each position’s hidden
vector to logits over the vocabulary |V|.
• Same forward module is used in training (parallel over positions) and
inference (often only last-position logits matter per step).

title: Teacher forcing vs. open-loop generation
text:
Teacher forcing vs. open-loop generation
Exposure bias (conceptual)
• Training: the model always sees the ground-truth prefix (teacher
forcing) — stable gradients, parallel across time in Transformers.
• Inference: the model eats its own previous predictions; early mistakes
can steer the trajectory away from the training distribution.
• This gap is called exposure bias. Mitigations include scheduled
sampling, RL-style fine-tuning (e.g. RLHF), or stronger decoding / better
models — not required detail for lab demos, but important for systems
thinking.

title: Inference
text:
Inference
Autoregressive decoding
1 Provide prompt tokens x1:p (may include <bos>).
2 Run forward pass; read logits at the last position p; sample or choose
arg max next token xp+1.
3 Append xp+1 to context; repeat until <eos>, stop string, or
max new tokens.
• Decoding knobs (temperature, top-k, nucleus, repetition): next slide.
• Cost grows with generated length (unlike one-shot image generators):
each new token usually needs another forward pass (KV-cache speeds
this up in practice).

title: Decoding hyperparameters
text:
Decoding hyperparameters
Temperature, top-k, top-p, repetition penalty
• Temperature T > 0: rescale logits zi ←zi/T before softmax.
• T < 1: sharper distribution ⇒closer to greedy / less diverse.
• T > 1: flatter distribution ⇒more random exploration (can improve
variety or add errors).
• Top-k: keep only the k largest logits (others −∞), then sample or
arg max within that set — caps how “wild” rare tokens can be.
• Top-p (nucleus sampling): sort tokens by probability mass; keep the
smallest prefix whose cumulative probability ≥p ∈(0, 1]; sample inside
that nucleus — adapts |S| per step (easy vs. hard contexts).
• Repetition penalty (e.g. HF-style): after forming logits, down-weight
scores for tokens that already appeared in the generated prefix (variants
differ on how much / which positions). Reduces loops; too strong ⇒
awkward paraphrase or drift.

title: Greedy vs. stochastic decoding
text:
Greedy vs. stochastic decoding
• Greedy / beam search: pick arg maxj (or keep several hypotheses with
beam search). Deterministic greedy can loop; beam search helps quality
in translation/summarization but costs more memory/compute.
• Stochastic: sample j ∼Cat(softmax(z)) after temperature / top-k /
top-p filtering — diverse outputs; set seed for reproducibility in
homework.
• Trade-off: greedy favors locally likely tokens; sampling explores but can
wander off-topic unless knobs tuned.

title: Inference efficiency
text:
Inference efficiency
KV-cache (idea)
• At step t, keys/values for earlier positions need not be recomputed from
scratch; frameworks cache past K/V tensors per layer (KV-cache) and
append for the new token.
• Effect: amortizes attention cost when generating long outputs (still linear
memory in sequence length × layers for the cache).
• Training usually computes full attention without this cache; generation
APIs enable use cache=True-style paths.

title: Toy example

Toy example
Character-level RNN generator
class CharRNNLM(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, vocab_size, embed_dim, hidden_size):
super().__init__()
self.embed = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim)
self.rnn = nn.GRU(embed_dim, hidden_size, batch_first=True)
self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_size, vocab_size)
def forward(self, x):
emb, _ = self.rnn(self.embed(x)) # x: (B, T)
logits = self.fc(emb) # (B, T, V)
return logits
• Training: teacher forcing on sequences and cross-entropy over vocabulary
(same shifted-label idea as GPT training).
• Generation: start from <bos>, feed back sampled characters step-by-step.
• Transformer counterpart + runnable script: text-gpt/
(train tinyshakespeare gpt.py).

title: LoRA: big picture
text:
LoRA: big picture
• Freeze most weights of a base LM; inject trainable low-rank matrices
into selected linear layers (often attention projections).
• Intuition: the task-specific update is approximated by a small matrix
factorization.
• At inference you can keep adapter separate (load peft adapter) or merge
into base weights if supported.

title: Notation: W 0 (frozen pretrained weights)
text:
Notation: W 0 (frozen pretrained weights)
• W 0 denotes the weight matrix of one linear map already learned during
pretraining (checkpoint), e.g. dense layers implementing projections.
• Shape W 0 ∈Rd×k: maps an input x ∈Rk to W 0x ∈Rd.
• During LoRA fine-tuning, entries of W 0 are typically frozen: no
gradients, no optimizer step on W 0.

title: Where does W 0 appear in an LLM?
text:
Where does W 0 appear in an LLM?
• A causal LM stack has many W 0-style matrices (not a single matrix for
the whole network).
• In each Transformer block, usual candidates are attention linear maps
(q proj, k proj, v proj, o proj / architecture-specific names) and
often feed-forward (gate proj, up proj, down proj) in GPT-style
blocks.
• LoRA does not attach automatically to “every” layer unless you
configure it so: libraries match parameter names via target modules.
The same name (e.g. q proj) repeats in every block ℓ= 1, . . . , L, so
one pattern can span all depths.

title: Notation: ∆W (trainable task adaptation)
text:
Notation: ∆W (trainable task adaptation)
• ∆W is the additive update we want on top of W 0 so the model fits
your downstream data.
• Low-rank factorization (few parameters):
∆W = BA,
A ∈Rr×k, B ∈Rd×r, r ≪min(d, k).
• Only A, B are trained (plus optional biases); W 0 stays fixed.
• Effective linear map used in the adapted layer:
x 7→W 0x + scaling · ∆W x (scaling uses lora alpha / r in common
implementations).

title: Effective weights on one targeted linear map
text:
Effective weights on one targeted linear map
Equation (symbols match one linear transformation)
W = W 0 + ∆W ,
∆W = BA.
This is repeated independently for each selected matrix (each has its own
A, B pair in code).
• Rank r: capacity of ∆W ; smaller r ⇒fewer adapter parameters (often
safer on small datasets).
• Forward implementation typically applies W 0x and adds a scaled
adapter term (lora alpha/r scaling in Hugging Face peft).

title: peft: main hyperparameters
text:
peft: main hyperparameters
• r: rank of ∆W for each injected adapter (r ↑⇒more expressive, more
trainable weights).
• lora alpha: scales how strongly ∆W can move outputs relative to
frozen W 0.
• lora dropout: dropout on the adapter branch (regularization).
• target modules: substring / name list deciding which linear matrices
get a ∆W ; you choose attention-only, attention+MLP, etc.; not “the
entire model” unless every module name matches.

title: Why Quantization?
text:
Why Quantization?
• LLMs are memory-bound: weights dominate VRAM usage.
• Example:
• 7B model (FP16) ≈14GB
• 13B model ≈26GB
• Key idea:
• Reduce precision →reduce memory
• Goal:
• Fit large models on small GPUs (T4, Colab)
• Enable efficient fine-tuning (QLoRA)

title: What “API access” means
text:
What “API access” means
• Your program sends HTTPS requests with prompt/messages; provider
runs model; returns text (or structured output).
• You pay per token (usually) and must handle rate limits, timeouts, and
errors.
• Many servers expose an OpenAI-compatible schema (same JSON
fields, different base url).

title: Checklist before coding
text:
Checklist before coding
1 Create API key; store in environment variable (OPENAI API KEY),
never commit to git.
2 Pick model name string allowed by your provider (e.g. gpt-4o-mini).
3 Decide parameters: temperature, max tokens, optional
response format.
4 Wrap calls with retries for HTTP 429 / transient errors.

title: Minimal pattern (Python)
text:
Minimal pattern (Python)
import os
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(
api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"],
base_url=os.environ.get("OPENAI_BASE_URL"),
)
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
model="gpt-4o-mini",
messages=[{"role":"user","content":"Hello!"}],
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)

title: Automation patterns (beyond one-off calls)
text:
Automation patterns (beyond one-off calls)
• Batch / loop: chunk inputs, sleep or throttle between calls.
• Structured output: ask for JSON in the prompt and json.loads after
(or use native JSON mode if available).
• Tools / function calling: model returns tool names + arguments; your
code executes tools and feeds results back.

title: Quick evaluation (pragmatic)
text:
Quick evaluation (pragmatic)
• Hold out a small validation set; compare loss or task accuracy / string
match rules.
• For generation: spot-check outputs, measure repetition, use a few
reference prompts shared across experiments.
• For APIs: log token usage if the provider exposes it; estimate cost per 1k
requests.

title: Safety and ethics (short)
text:
Safety and ethics (short)
• Do not paste secrets or personal data into third-party APIs without
policy approval.
• Generated text can be wrong or biased — add human review for
high-stakes use.
• Respect provider terms of use and course rules on assisted work /
plagiarism.

title: Summary
text:
Summary
What to remember
Core ideas
• Generative text (this deck, opening section): AR factorization;
tokenizer →ids; shifted next-token training; decoding (temperature,
top-k, top-p); KV-cache; samples under 10-modern-llms/samples/.
• LoRA: train small adapters on top of a frozen base; configure r, alpha,
target modules.
• QLoRA: quantized base + LoRA + k-bit training helpers; needs GPU
tooling (bitsandbytes).
• APIs: keys in env, handle rate limits, structure messages, plan for cost
and failures.
• Samples: 10-modern-llms/samples/ (lora minimal.py,
qlora train minimal.py, api chat minimal.py).
